newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Europe's airlines urge EU to help keep prices down.
newsitem.headline: Europe's airlines urge EU to help keep prices down.

text.p: Europe's airlines, meeting to discuss their future as the European Union's liberalisation of their industry nears completion, on Friday urged EU action to ensure they remain global competitors.

The Association of European Airlines (AEA) said at its annual meeting in Dublin that the most critical issue facing its members was the inefficiency of Europe's traffic control network, which was burdening airlines with huge costs.

Herbert Bammer, chairman of the AEA, which represents 26 European carriers, said an overhaul of European air-traffic control was required, leading to the creation of a unified system for the continent.
He said at a news conference that the current system's inefficiencies were costing Europe's airlines 2.5 billion Ecus ($3.2 billion) a year and adding eight percent to the cost of air tickets.
"The air traffic management is the most urgent issue, because it costs us a lot of money which is wasted; it costs our customers; and it has a very negative effect on the environment," Bammer said.

Gary McGann, chief executive of Irish national carrier Aer Lingus, said the EU's representatives at the meeting were urged to ensure that airlines were not faced with rising costs at a time they were trying to cut prices.
He said the full benefits of the EU's liberalisation programme, due to be completed in April 1997, would only be realized if airlines' costs were kept down.

"Our focus is on improving the efficiency and the pricing to our customers of the products we deliver, and at the same time to achieve a profit for the airlines so they can continue to be sucessful," McGann said.

The AEA said charges levied by airports had to be regulated to keep costs down. "Management of airports should become a top priority," it said. "Airport charges should be transparent and strictly related to services which airlines require."

It warned the EU against meddling unduly in airlines' commercial affairs. "The European authorities have presented the airlines with the fact of liberalisation, and the airlines are responding to it positively with more competition, more routes and lower fares," it said.
"The authorities should not intervene more than absolutely necessary in the policies the airlines have chosen to adopt in making use of the possibilities that liberalisation offers."
The airlines also called for European action to tackle the worsening problem of airport congestion.
"Many European airports are already crowded, and the problem will become chronic in the near future," they said.
"The European authorities should be looking at ways to speed up growth in capacity at hub airports since decisions cannot be left at a local level."

Emmet Stagg, a minister at Ireland's transport ministry, represented the EU at the meeting as Ireland currently holds the presidency of the 15-nation group. He said the EU recognised its role in upholding the competitiveness of European airlines.

"As airlines continue to restructure and reorganise in order to reduce their costs, regulators must focus their efforts on the impact of costs external to airlines on the competitiveness of the European aviation sector," Stagg said.
